binary-anatomy.core: Linux binaries are ELF files: headers describe architecture and segments, and sections hold code (.text), constants (.rodata), data (.data, .bss), symbols and debug info. Compilers emit objects with relocations, the linker resolves symbols statically or records shared dependencies, ld.so loads and relocates libraries at runtime (hookable with LD_PRELOAD), and the vDSO serves hot syscalls in user space.

first_principles.problem: Exec format errors, missing libraries and bloated binaries are mysterious without ELF knowledge.

analogy.title: A flat-pack kit assembled on arrival
analogy.story: Labels, parts and a stage manager gathering pieces.
analogy.breaks: Kits don't download parts; dynamic binaries do.

check.q: What program actually loads shared libraries for a dynamically linked binary?
check.a: The dynamic loader (ld-linux.so), named in the binary's PT_INTERP header.

cli-literacy.core: CLI literacy means understanding the shell as a parser that launches processes with streams and exit codes. Core navigation, reading, finding and inspection tools combine through pipes; redirection controls stdout and stderr; ps and signals manage processes gracefully; startup files differ by shell mode; SSH keys sign challenges for secure access; and tmux keeps sessions alive across disconnects.

first_principles.problem: Engineers copy commands without understanding, then can't debug failures.

analogy.title: A precise conversation with the OS
analogy.story: Clear instructions, checked replies, chained tasks.

check.q: What three things does every process launched by the shell receive?
check.a: Arguments, environment variables and standard file descriptors (stdin, stdout, stderr), and it returns an exit code.

cloud-init.core: cloud-init gives generic cloud images an identity at first boot. It reads metadata and user-data (cloud-config YAML, scripts or multipart), runs modules in fixed stages (local, network, config, final), and leaves detailed logs and state. When SSH is broken, console output, serial consoles, SSM or rescue volumes let you debug.

first_principles.problem: Manual post-boot configuration doesn't scale and drifts.

analogy.title: A welcome pack for every new machine
analogy.story: Read on arrival; set up accordingly.
analogy.breaks: People remember; cloud-init tracks per instance.

example.title: Fleet bootstrap
flow: Console output checked in CI smoke test

check.q: Why prefer cloud-config over a bash user-data script?
check.a: It's declarative, readable and uses idempotent modules for common tasks, reducing fragile imperative logic.

filesystem-integrity.core: Filesystems must survive torn multi-block updates and lying caches. Journaling logs intent and replays after crashes, copy-on-write never overwrites live data and switches roots atomically, barriers and fsync enforce ordering and durability, block checksums with redundancy detect and heal bit rot, and snapshots give instant rollback and consistent backups but don't replace off-host copies.

first_principles.problem: Crashes and silent corruption destroy data integrity.

analogy.title: A ledger, sealed envelopes and bookmarks
analogy.story: Record intent, detect tampering, and keep points to return to.

check.q: Which two mechanisms let filesystems recover consistency after a crash?
check.a: Journaling (replaying a write-ahead log) and copy-on-write (atomically switching to a fully written new tree).

gpu-kernel-interactions.core: A GPU is a separate computer driven by the CPU through a kernel and user-space driver stack. Performance depends on feeding it, PCIe and NUMA locality, NVLink versus PCIe for multi-GPU sync, GPUDirect RDMA for multi-node transfers and careful use of unified memory. nvidia-smi and topo -m reveal utilisation, throttling and topology, and Xid errors separate application bugs from failing hardware.

first_principles.problem: Expensive GPUs sit underused or fail mysteriously.

analogy.title: A factory next door with trucks and hotlines
analogy.story: Keep trucks moving, use hotlines between factories, watch warning lights.

check.q: Name three common causes of poor GPU performance besides model code.
check.a: Data loading starvation, poor PCIe/NUMA locality, slow inter-GPU interconnect (or power/thermal throttling).

hardware-sympathy.core: Hardware sympathy means coding for how CPUs and memory really work. Memory is roughly 100× slower than L1 cache; data moves in 64-byte lines that reward contiguous layouts; false sharing makes unrelated writes contend; NUMA makes remote memory slower; branch mispredictions flush pipelines; and speculation creates side channels whose mitigations cost performance. Profile with counters, then fix data layout first.

first_principles.problem: Code with good Big-O still runs slowly on real hardware.

analogy.title: A driver who understands the engine
analogy.story: Shift with the machine, not against it.

check.q: What is typically the biggest lever for CPU performance in data-heavy code?
check.a: Memory access patterns and data layout, keeping hot data contiguous and in cache.

hugepages.core: 4 KB pages force large-memory applications into constant TLB misses and page walks, because TLB reach is entries × page size. Huge pages (2 MB, 1 GB) multiply reach. Explicit hugetlbfs pages are reserved and predictable, THP is automatic but can stall (prefer madvise), and 1 GB pages need boot-time reservation. Size pools precisely and configure apps like PostgreSQL and the JVM to use them.

first_principles.problem: Big heaps waste CPU on address translation.

analogy.title: Postcodes instead of house numbers
analogy.story: Fewer entries in the address book.

example.title: DB host tuning
flow: Reserve 2 MB pool sized to shared_buffers

check.q: What are the trade-offs between explicit huge pages and THP?
check.a: Explicit pages are guaranteed and predictable but must be reserved and sized; THP is automatic but can cause compaction stalls and bloat.

inspection-tools.core: Go beyond top: lscpu and lstopo reveal sockets, cores, SMT siblings, caches and device locality for pinning; slabtop and /proc/meminfo expose kernel slab memory and leaks; and /proc/<pid>/smaps gives per-mapping memory with PSS for fair accounting and private dirty pages for true ownership.

first_principles.problem: Summary tools hide where CPU and memory really go.

analogy.title: Floor plans and utility meters
analogy.story: Not just who's there, but where resources go.

example.title: Memory mystery solved
flow: Reclaimable; workload creates millions of temp files

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Fix root cause, not RAM size.

check.q: Which measure best represents a process's fair share of memory?
check.a: PSS (proportional set size), which divides shared pages among the processes sharing them.

interrupt-handling.core: Interrupts let devices signal CPUs but get costly at high rates. Linux splits work into short top halves and deferred bottom halves (softirqs, overflowing to ksoftirqd), NAPI switches network receive from interrupts to budgeted polling under load to avoid livelock, and IRQ affinity spreads queue interrupts across NUMA-local cores while isolating latency-critical ones.

first_principles.problem: Interrupt storms saturate single cores and drop packets.

analogy.title: A doorbell, receptionist and back office
analogy.story: Answer fast, process later, batch when busy, share the load.

example.title: Network host tuning
flow: 16 queues, IRQs pinned to node-local cores

check.q: What are the two main techniques to prevent one CPU from being overwhelmed by network interrupts?
check.a: Spreading queue IRQs across cores (RSS/affinity) and NAPI polling to batch processing under load.

ipc-mechanisms.core: Isolated processes communicate through kernel-mediated IPC. Pipes and FIFOs give backpressured byte streams; signals give payload-less async notifications that need minimal handlers; Unix sockets give fast local client/server with permissions, credentials and FD passing; shared memory gives zero-copy exchange at the cost of DIY synchronisation; and mmap treats files as memory via the page cache.

first_principles.problem: Wrong IPC choices waste CPU and add latency or bugs.

analogy.title: Neighbours' communication options
analogy.story: Notes, knocks, intercom, shared board.

example.title: Local architecture
flow: Video workers share frames via shm ring

check.q: Which IPC mechanism offers the lowest latency for bulk data between local processes?
check.a: Shared memory (including mmap of shared files), since no kernel copies are needed.

linux-boot-process.core: Linux boots as a relay. UEFI or BIOS finds the bootloader; GRUB loads the kernel and initramfs with a command line; the kernel initialises hardware and runs the initramfs, which assembles storage and switch_roots to the real root; and systemd as PID 1 starts units in parallel to reach the target. Each stage's symptoms and tools pinpoint failures.

first_principles.problem: Boot failures are opaque without stage awareness.

analogy.title: A relay race
analogy.story: Know each handoff to know where the baton fell.
analogy.breaks: Races are visible; boot is mostly hidden.

check.q: Which file system image bridges the kernel and the real root filesystem?
check.a: The initramfs, a temporary RAM-based root that prepares and mounts the real root.

linux-filesystem.core: Linux's filesystem model rests on 'everything is a file'. Inodes hold metadata separate from names (and can run out), file descriptors are per-process handles with limits, hard links share inodes while symlinks store paths, the FHS defines where things belong, mounts attach filesystems into one tree with protective options, and /proc and /sys expose live kernel state as files.

first_principles.problem: Storage errors, FD leaks and misplaced data are confusing without the model.

analogy.title: A universal adaptor plus a library catalogue
analogy.story: One interface and careful records.

check.q: Name two resources besides disk space that can be exhausted on a Linux filesystem/process.
check.a: Inodes (filesystem) and file descriptors (per process/system).

linux-kernel-scheduling.core: The Linux scheduler arbitrates cores via strictly ordered classes. CFS (now EEVDF) shares fairly by weight using vruntime; context switches carry hidden cache costs; preemption models trade throughput for latency; real-time policies (FIFO, RR, DEADLINE) with core isolation and locked memory give bounded latency; and affinity with NUMA awareness keeps tasks near caches and memory.

first_principles.problem: Mixed workloads interfere and latency becomes unpredictable.

analogy.title: A traffic cop with priority lanes
analogy.story: Emergency lanes, fair turns, and keeping cars near their exits.

example.title: Mixed host
flow: Audio thread SCHED_FIFO on isolated core

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Each workload gets what it needs.

check.q: Which scheduling policy guarantees a task a CPU budget per period?
check.a: SCHED_DEADLINE, using runtime, deadline and period with admission control.

linux-memory-management.core: Linux memory is a managed illusion. Virtual pages map to frames via page tables, faults fill mappings lazily (minor in memory, major from disk), overcommit grants promises that may exceed RAM, swap holds cold anonymous pages with swappiness biasing reclaim, and the OOM killer kills by score when reclaim fails, which cgroups, score adjustments and PSI-driven userspace killers can shape. Visibility needs several tools.

first_principles.problem: Memory numbers confuse, and pressure leads to surprises.

analogy.title: An overbooked hotel with a storage annex
analogy.story: Rooms assigned on arrival, extras stored away, and someone bumped if full.

check.q: What decides which process the kernel OOM killer terminates?
check.a: The highest oom_score, mainly based on memory usage share and adjusted by oom_score_adj.

linux-observability-ebpf.core: Linux observability tools see inside running systems. strace exposes syscalls at high cost, tcpdump gives packet ground truth, perf samples stacks and counts hardware events for flame graphs, and eBPF runs verified, JIT-compiled programs at kernel and user hooks, aggregating in maps with low overhead, through ready-made BCC tools and ad-hoc bpftrace scripts.

first_principles.problem: Production issues need visibility without redeploys or heavy overhead.

analogy.title: Medical imaging for systems
analogy.story: Different scanners for different questions, no surgery needed.
analogy.breaks: Imaging is passive; some tools slow the patient.

check.q: What makes eBPF safe to run in the kernel?
check.a: The verifier statically proves programs terminate, access memory within bounds and only use permitted helpers before JIT compilation.

linux-permissions.core: Linux permissions check the process's UID and GIDs against each file's owner, group and rwx bits, and directory bits mean list, create or delete, and traverse. chmod (symbolic or octal) and chown set modes and ownership, umask sets defaults, setuid, setgid and sticky add special behaviours (with setuid a key escalation risk), and ACLs add named principals and inheritance. Grant least privilege, never 777.

first_principles.problem: Permission errors tempt dangerous fixes like 777 or setuid scripts.

analogy.title: Keycards and floor rules
analogy.story: Right card for the right room, special rules where needed.
analogy.breaks: Keycards are physical; permissions are bits.

check.q: What three mechanisms help a team share a directory safely?
check.a: Group ownership with setgid on the directory, group write with an appropriate umask (e.g. 002), and the sticky bit to stop deleting others' files.

linux-resource-management.core: Linux shares resources among processes and provides three control layers. ulimits are per-process soft and hard quotas (set via systemd for services), cgroups are hierarchical budgets for CPU, memory, I/O and PIDs (unified in v2) with accounting, and namespaces give isolated views. Docker combines them with security layers, and hidden kernel limits like backlogs, conntrack and FDs can silently drop traffic.

first_principles.problem: Noisy neighbours and invisible limits cause outages.

analogy.title: Flat rules, meters and private rooms
analogy.story: Fair sharing in a shared building.

example.title: Host hardening
flow: Services in slices with CPU/memory limits

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: No noisy neighbours or silent drops.

check.q: Which mechanism should you use to cap a systemd service's memory?
check.a: A cgroup limit via systemd (MemoryMax= / MemoryHigh=), not ulimit.

linux-security-modules.core: The LSM framework hooks kernel operations so modules can enforce mandatory access control beyond owner-controlled DAC, binding even root. SELinux uses labels, type enforcement and modes, with AVC denials decoded via audit2why and fixed by restorecon, fcontext, booleans or ports before any custom modules. AppArmor offers simpler path-based profiles with complain and enforce modes. Keep MAC enforcing to contain compromises.

first_principles.problem: DAC can't contain compromised services, especially as root.

analogy.title: Central security on top of door keys
analogy.story: Even key-holders can't go everywhere.

check.q: What's the recommended first step when SELinux blocks a legitimate action?
check.a: Check and restore file labels (restorecon / semanage fcontext), the most common cause, before booleans or custom policy.

linux-timekeeping.core: Linux time comes from a drifting RTC and a high-resolution clocksource, disciplined by NTP (chrony) that slews rather than steps. Use wall-clock time for timestamps and monotonic time for durations, handle leap seconds with consistent smeared sources, and use time namespaces to offset monotonic clocks for container migration.

first_principles.problem: Clock skew breaks logs, distributed systems and timeouts.

analogy.title: Watches synced to a radio signal, plus stopwatches
analogy.story: Accurate time of day and reliable elapsed time.
analogy.breaks: Watches don't jump; system clocks can.

check.q: Which clock should be used to measure request latency and why?
check.a: CLOCK_MONOTONIC, because it never jumps backward or forward when wall-clock time is corrected.

networking-scaling.core: One NIC queue makes one core the network bottleneck. RSS hashes flows to multiple hardware queues pinned to cores, RPS does the same in software for limited NICs, RFS steers flows to the CPU running their consumer for cache locality, and XPS gives each CPU its own transmit queue to avoid lock contention, all while preserving per-flow ordering.

first_principles.problem: Fast NICs are capped by single-core packet processing.

analogy.title: More toll booths with smart lane assignment
analogy.story: Spread traffic, keep each car in its lane, send it near its exit.

example.title: 25 Gbps host
flow: 16 RSS queues pinned to node-local cores

check.q: Which technique spreads receive processing in hardware, and which in software?
check.a: RSS in hardware (NIC queues); RPS in software (kernel steering).

process-internals.core: A process is a bundle of address space, threads, FDs, credentials and limits. It's born by fork with copy-on-write, transformed by exec (FDs persist unless CLOEXEC), and dies by exit with status reaped via wait, or lingers as a zombie. States (R, S, D, Z) reveal behaviour, signals notify it (TERM to drain, HUP to reload, KILL as the uncatchable last resort), and load average counts R plus D tasks.

first_principles.problem: Hung, zombie or ungraceful processes cause outages and confusion.

analogy.title: A workshop's life
analogy.story: Opened from a template, refitted, closed with paperwork, and staff states visible.

example.title: Healthy container
flow: Load vs nproc monitored with PSI

check.q: What creates a zombie process?
check.a: A child that has exited but whose parent hasn't yet called wait() to collect its exit status.

psi-metrics.core: PSI replaces ambiguous load average with direct stall measurements per resource. /proc/pressure reports 'some' (any task delayed) and 'full' (no progress) for CPU, memory and I/O over 10, 60 and 300 seconds plus cumulative totals and triggers. CPU pressure reveals run-queue contention and quota throttling, memory pressure warns of thrashing before OOM, I/O pressure exposes storage contention, and per-cgroup files scope all of it to workloads.

first_principles.problem: Load average can't tell which resource hurts which workload.

analogy.title: Queue timers per department and resource
analogy.story: Know exactly who waits for what.

check.q: Which PSI value is the strongest sign of severe resource starvation?
check.a: A high 'full' value, meaning all non-idle tasks were stalled simultaneously.

storage-io-path.core: A write passes the VFS, filesystem and page cache before writeback, the block layer and the device, so durability needs fsync. Buffered I/O uses the page cache while direct I/O bypasses it for self-caching apps. I/O APIs evolved from blocking calls through select and poll (O(n)) and epoll (O(ready) readiness) to io_uring (batched completion rings). blk-mq queues, queue depth and the right scheduler (none for NVMe) determine device performance.

first_principles.problem: Durability bugs, scalability limits and underused devices come from misunderstanding the I/O path.

analogy.title: Postal system from postbox to doorstep
analogy.story: Collection, sorting, routing and a signed receipt.
analogy.breaks: Post is slow; I/O is microseconds.

check.q: Which Linux I/O API supports true asynchronous file I/O with batching?
check.a: io_uring.

system-tuning.core: Runtime kernel tuning via sysctl must be driven by measurement. Classify bottlenecks as CPU-bound or I/O-bound, read load average relative to cores (or prefer PSI), tune VM settings (swappiness, byte-based dirty limits) and network settings (backlogs, ports, buffers, conntrack) for the workload, and keep Magic SysRq for emergency diagnostics and safe reboots.

first_principles.problem: Copy-pasted tuning and misread metrics cause instability.

analogy.title: A mixing desk with an emergency stop
analogy.story: Deliberate tweaks while listening, and a safe off switch.

example.title: Tuning review
flow: All in sysctl.d with ticket refs

check.q: What's the most important rule of kernel tuning?
check.a: Change settings only in response to measured bottlenecks, one at a time, verifying the effect.

systemd-basics.core: systemd is PID 1 and the service manager. Unit files declare services (with the right Type=, restart policy and sandboxing), timers, sockets, mounts and slices; dependencies separate requirement (Wants, Requires) from ordering (After); targets group system states; journald centralises logs; drop-ins customise units safely; and masking forbids units entirely.

first_principles.problem: Ad-hoc scripts lack supervision, ordering and logs.

analogy.title: An orchestra conductor with a score
analogy.story: Cues, recovery and a recording of the performance.

check.q: What tool should you use to customise a vendor unit without editing it?
check.a: systemctl edit <unit>, which creates a drop-in override in /etc/systemd/system/<unit>.d/.

systemtap-tracing.core: SystemTap was Linux's dynamic tracer before eBPF. Scripts of probes and handlers pass through parse, elaborate, translate, compile and run into kernel modules that need debuginfo; tapsets give stable probe aliases; safe mode limits risk while guru mode removes guardrails. Today it's mainly for older kernels, with bpftrace and eBPF as safer successors.

first_principles.problem: Older kernels need dynamic tracing without eBPF.

analogy.title: An older, heavier diagnostic machine
analogy.story: Capable, but needs setup and care.

example.title: RHEL 7 investigation
flow: Build module on staging with debuginfo
Unload; plan upgrade to eBPF-capable kernel

check.q: What prerequisite makes SystemTap heavier to deploy than bpftrace?
check.a: It needs matching kernel debuginfo, headers and a compiler to build a kernel module for each script.

virtualization-primitives.core: Hypervisors share hardware among VMs with CPU and memory virtualisation assists. Steal time reveals host CPU contention, ballooning and two-level page tables shape guest memory, virtio paravirtual devices give near-native I/O through shared rings, and thin-provisioned storage enables overcommit but risks pool exhaustion. Monitor host-level reality, not just the guest's view.

first_principles.problem: VM performance mysteries come from hidden host contention.

analogy.title: Apartments sharing building systems
analogy.story: Your flat is fine until the plumbing is overloaded.

check.q: Which metric reveals that a VM is being starved by its hypervisor?
check.a: CPU steal time (st / %steal).

windows-server-basics.core: Hybrid fleets need Windows fluency. PowerShell passes objects not text, the registry replaces /etc and should be managed as code, NTFS ACLs combine with share permissions (most restrictive wins), Active Directory centralises identity and Group Policy (protect Tier 0), and IIS app pools isolate sites while RDP needs strict protection.

first_principles.problem: Linux-centric teams struggle to operate Windows services.

analogy.title: Driving on the other side
analogy.story: Same car, different controls.
analogy.breaks: Cars are similar; object pipelines differ.

check.q: What makes PowerShell pipelines fundamentally different from Unix shell pipelines?
check.a: They pass structured .NET objects with properties rather than plain text streams.
